_readme: MEHRAN glossary — original wording written for this simulator. clo = course learning outcome tag (CLO1 concepts & governance, CLO2 planning & control techniques, CLO3 people, stakeholders, agile & AI). Formulas follow standard PM practice.

terms.definition: A temporary endeavour with a definite start and end, undertaken to create a unique product, service or result. Temporary refers to the effort, not to the outcome: a runway lasts decades, the project that builds it does not.
Ongoing, repetitive work that sustains an organisation, such as running the airport day to day after handover. Projects change things; operations keep them running.
Applying knowledge, skills, tools and techniques to project activities so that the project meets its requirements and delivers the intended value.
The person assigned by the performing organisation to lead the team responsible for achieving the project objectives. Accountable for integration, but not the owner of the business case.
The senior person or group who provides resources and support, owns the business case, and is the escalation point for decisions outside the project manager's authority.

A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge, the PMI standard describing principles, performance domains and practices. The 8th edition frames the discipline around principles, performance domains and focus areas, and treats delivery approaches (predictive, agile, hybrid) as tailoring choices.
A foundational norm that guides behaviour across every project, regardless of approach. Principles are not processes: they tell you how to think when the processes do not cover the situation.
Principle: treat the project as a system of interacting parts (scope, schedule, cost, people, risk, environment) and consider how a change in one ripples through the others before acting.
Principle: judge decisions by the value they create for the sponsor, users and society, not merely by finishing tasks. Output is not the same as outcome.
Principle: build quality into processes and deliverables from the start rather than inspecting it in at the end. Prevention costs less than failure.
Principle: leaders take ownership of outcomes, act ethically, communicate openly and create the conditions for the team to succeed.
Principle: weigh the environmental, social and economic effects of the project across its whole life cycle — for an airport, noise, dust, energy, water and community impacts as well as cost.
Principle: create an environment of trust, psychological safety and shared ownership in which team members can decide, speak up and improve how work is done.

A group of related activities critical to delivering project outcomes. In the PMBOK 8th edition the seven domains are Governance, Scope, Schedule, Finance, Stakeholders, Resources and Risk. They interact continuously rather than running in sequence.
Performance domain covering the decision rights, oversight, policies, gates and escalation paths that keep the project aligned with organisational strategy.
Performance domain covering estimating, budgeting, funding, cost control and financial forecasting, including earned value management and reserves.
In the PMBOK 8th edition, a grouping of work by purpose — Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring and Controlling, Closing. Focus areas overlap in time; they are not strict phases.
The earlier PMBOK term for the five logical groupings of processes: Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring and Controlling, Closing.
Focus area that defines a new project or phase and obtains authorisation: business case review, charter, initial stakeholder identification.
Focus area that establishes scope, refines objectives and defines the course of action: WBS, schedule, budget, risk, quality, communications and procurement plans.
Focus area that completes the work defined in the plan: directing the team, managing quality, procurement, communications and stakeholder engagement.
Focus area that tracks, reviews and regulates progress and performance, identifies variances and initiates corrective or preventive action through change control.
Focus area that formally completes the project or phase: acceptance, contract closure, lessons learned, archiving and release of resources.
The series of phases a project passes through from start to completion. It can be predictive, iterative, incremental, adaptive or hybrid.

A delivery approach in which scope, schedule and cost are determined early and change is managed formally — appropriate for well-understood, high-consequence work such as pavement and airfield lighting.
Informal name for a sequential predictive life cycle in which each phase finishes before the next begins.

A delivery approach (agile, iterative or incremental) in which requirements are elaborated during delivery through short feedback cycles — suited to uncertain work such as passenger-facing digital systems.
A combination of predictive and adaptive elements, chosen per work package. In this simulator the civil works are predictive while terminal IT and wayfinding are agile.
Deliberately adapting the approach, governance and processes to suit the project, its environment and its risks, rather than applying a method mechanically.
A documented economic feasibility study that justifies the project by comparing benefits, costs, risks and options. It is the reference for every later go/no-go decision.
Ensuring that the outcomes promised in the business case are actually achieved after handover, measured with agreed indicators (for an airport: movements, passengers, punctuality).
The present value of future cash inflows minus the present value of outflows, discounted at a chosen rate. A positive NPV indicates the investment adds value at that rate.
The discount rate at which a project's NPV equals zero. Higher is better when comparing options of similar risk.
The time needed for cumulative net cash inflows to recover the initial investment. Simple to explain, but it ignores the time value of money and benefits after payback.

The document issued by the sponsor that formally authorises the project and gives the project manager authority to apply organisational resources. It records purpose, high-level requirements, milestones, budget and key stakeholders.
The integrated document that describes how the project will be executed, monitored, controlled and closed. It contains the baselines and the subsidiary management plans.
The approved, integrated scope-schedule-cost baseline against which execution is measured. Changes to it go through formal change control.
An approved version of a work product (scope, schedule or cost) used as the basis for comparison. Changing a baseline requires an approved change request.
Formally replacing a baseline after an approved major change. Done too often it hides poor performance; never done, it leaves the team measuring against a fiction.
Conditions outside the project team's control that influence the project — regulation, market conditions, climate, culture, infrastructure. Heat, dust storms and monsoon rain are EEFs at Hyderabad.
Plans, processes, policies, templates and knowledge bases specific to the performing organisation, including lessons learned from earlier projects.
An organisational unit that standardises project governance and facilitates sharing of resources, methods and tools. It can be supportive, controlling or directive.

A group of related projects and programme activities managed in a coordinated way to obtain benefits not available from managing them individually — for example a runway, terminal and access-road project delivered together.
Projects, programmes and operations managed as a group to achieve strategic objectives. Portfolio management decides which projects to do at all.
A review at the end of a phase where performance and the business case are checked and a decision is made to continue, modify or stop. Also called a stage gate or kill point.
Coordinating all aspects of the project so that scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources, risks and stakeholders fit together. The project manager is the integrator.
Seeing the project as interacting feedback loops: adding labour to a crowded work face can lower output; deferring maintenance raises later failure costs.
The sum of the products, services and results to be provided as a project (product scope) and the work needed to deliver them (project scope).
Conditions or capabilities that must be present in a deliverable to satisfy an agreement or need. Good requirements are testable and traceable to a source.
A grid linking each requirement to its source, the WBS elements that deliver it and the test that verifies it, so nothing is lost or gold-plated.
A hierarchical decomposition of the total scope of work into deliverables and work packages. The 100% rule says the children of each element add up to exactly the parent.
The lowest level of the WBS, at which cost and duration can be estimated and managed and which has a single owner.
A document giving the detail for each WBS element: description, deliverables, acceptance criteria, owner, assumptions and associated risks.
WBS rule that the work at each level must represent 100% of the work of its parent — no more and no less.
A management control point where scope, budget and schedule are integrated and compared to earned value. It contains one or more work packages.
Uncontrolled expansion of scope without adjustment of time, cost and resources. The cure is integrated change control, not saying no to everything.
Adding features beyond the agreed requirements, usually by the team, without a change request. It consumes contingency and adds risk.
The conditions a deliverable must satisfy before it is accepted. For a runway section: friction, roughness and compaction within specification.
Formalising acceptance of completed deliverables with the customer or sponsor. Control Quality checks correctness; Validate Scope checks acceptance.
Iterative planning in which near-term work is planned in detail and later work at a higher level, refined as information emerges.
Continuously improving and detailing a plan as more specific information and more accurate estimates become available.
Any unique, verifiable product, result or capability that must be produced to complete a process, phase or project.
A scheduling technique that computes early and late start and finish dates with forward and backward passes, finds total float, and identifies the longest path through the network.
terms.formula: ES/EF forward pass; LS/LF backward pass; TF = LS − ES

terms.definition: The longest sequence of dependent activities through the network; it determines the shortest possible project duration. Any delay on it delays the finish unless recovered.
A path whose total float is small enough that a modest slip would make it critical. Crashing the critical path too far often hands the role to a near-critical path.
The amount of time an activity can be delayed from its early start without delaying the project finish date. Critical activities have zero (or the least) total float.
The amount of time an activity can be delayed without delaying the early start of any successor.
Calculation through the network from start to finish that determines early start and early finish dates.
terms.formula: EF = ES + duration; ES = max(EF of predecessors)

terms.definition: Calculation from the finish back to the start that determines late start and late finish dates.
terms.formula: LS = LF − duration; LF = min(LS of successors)

terms.definition: Activity-on-node network technique using four dependency types: finish-to-start, start-to-start, finish-to-finish and start-to-finish.
The most common dependency: the successor cannot start until the predecessor finishes (e.g. base course before asphalt surfacing).
The successor cannot start until the predecessor has started; often used with a lag for overlapping work.
The successor cannot finish until the predecessor has finished — e.g. testing cannot finish before installation finishes.
The rarest dependency: the successor cannot finish until the predecessor starts, such as an old system running until the new one starts.
A mandated delay between a predecessor and its successor (e.g. concrete curing time).
An acceleration that lets a successor begin before its predecessor is complete; a negative lag.
A dependency inherent in the nature of the work or required contractually — hard logic, such as foundations before columns.
A dependency chosen by the team based on best practice; it can be relaxed when fast-tracking. Also called preferred or soft logic.
A dependency on something outside the project, such as a regulator's inspection or a utility diversion.
A significant point or event in the project with zero duration, such as runway handover or terminal opening.
A bar chart of schedule information with activities on the vertical axis, dates on the horizontal axis and bars showing durations.
A summary schedule that shows only milestones — useful for sponsors and regulators.
Compressing the schedule by adding resources to critical activities at the lowest cost per day saved. Only critical-path activities are worth crashing.
terms.formula: Cost slope = (crash cost − normal cost) / (normal duration − crash duration)

terms.definition: The extra cost of shortening an activity by one day. Crash the cheapest critical activity first, and re-check the critical path after each step.
Compressing the schedule by doing activities in parallel that were planned in sequence. Costs little up front but increases risk and potential rework.
Techniques to shorten the schedule without reducing scope: crashing and fast-tracking.
Adjusting start and finish dates to balance demand with supply. It can extend the critical path.
Adjusting activities within their float so resource demand stays within limits without changing the critical path or finish date.
When a resource is assigned more work than it can do in the time available (demand above capacity). Fix with levelling, extra supply or re-sequencing.
A bar chart showing resource demand per period against capacity; peaks above the line indicate over-allocation.

Programme Evaluation and Review Technique: estimates activity duration from optimistic, most likely and pessimistic values using a weighted (beta) average and estimates uncertainty with a standard deviation.
Estimating with optimistic (O), most likely (M) and pessimistic (P) values. The triangular mean is (O+M+P)/3; the PERT beta mean is (O+4M+P)/6.
A measure of spread. For a path, PERT adds activity variances (σ²) and takes the square root; about 68% of outcomes fall within ±1σ, 95% within ±2σ, 99.7% within ±3σ.
Top-down estimating that uses actual values from a similar past project. Quick and cheap, but only as accurate as the analogy.
Estimating with a statistical relationship between historical data and variables, e.g. cost per square metre of pavement multiplied by area.
Estimating each work package in detail and rolling the estimates up the WBS. Most accurate and most expensive to prepare.
Running the schedule or cost model thousands of times with durations drawn from their distributions to obtain a probability distribution of outcomes (P10, P50, P80…).
Percentile outcomes from a Monte Carlo run: there is a 50% (or 80%) chance of finishing on or before that date or cost. Commit to P80 when the sponsor needs a date they can rely on.
The probability that the actual outcome will be at or below a given estimate. A higher confidence level requires a larger reserve.
A sensitivity chart that ranks variables by their influence on an outcome, with the widest bar at the top — it shows which estimates matter most.
Determining which risks or variables have the most potential impact on outcomes by varying one input at a time.
The earned-schedule version of schedule variance, expressed in time units rather than money, so it stays meaningful late in the project.
The time at which the current earned value should have been earned according to the baseline. It converts EV into time and fixes SPI's drift to 1.0 at the end.
Reviewing leads and lags to find legitimate overlaps or required waiting times when optimising the schedule.
An integrated method for measuring performance that compares planned value, earned value and actual cost to compute variances, indices and forecasts.
terms.formula: SV = EV − PV; CV = EV − AC; SPI = EV/PV; CPI = EV/AC

terms.definition: The authorised budget assigned to the work scheduled to be done by a given date. Also called BCWS.
The budgeted value of the work actually completed by a given date. Also called BCWP. It is the only measure that tells you how much work is really done.
The realised cost incurred for the work performed by a given date. Also called ACWP.
The total budget established for all the work to be performed (excluding management reserve).
The amount by which the project is ahead of or behind the planned delivery, in money terms. Negative means behind.
The budget deficit or surplus at a point in time. Negative means over budget.
A measure of schedule efficiency: value earned per unit of value planned. Below 1.0 means behind schedule; SPI 0.9 means only 90% of the planned work has been done.

A measure of cost efficiency: value earned per rupee spent. Below 1.0 means over budget; CPI 0.9 means every PKR 1 spent earns only PKR 0.90 of work. It is the most stable early predictor of final cost.
The expected total cost of completing all the work. Choose the formula that matches your assumption about future performance.
terms.formula: EAC = BAC/CPI (typical) · AC + (BAC − EV) (atypical) · AC + (BAC − EV)/(CPI × SPI) (composite) · AC + bottom-up ETC

terms.definition: The expected cost to finish all the remaining work.
The projected budget surplus or deficit at the end of the project. Negative means a forecast overrun.
The cost efficiency that must be achieved on the remaining work to meet a target (BAC or an approved EAC). TCPI above 1.10 against BAC is usually unrealistic.
terms.formula: TCPI(BAC) = (BAC − EV) / (BAC − AC); TCPI(EAC) = (BAC − EV) / (EAC − AC)

terms.definition: A graph of cumulative cost or progress over time; PV, EV and AC are usually plotted as S-curves to visualise variances.
Budget (or time) within the cost baseline for identified risks — the known-unknowns. The project manager draws on it as risks occur.
Budget outside the cost baseline but inside the total budget, held by the sponsor for unknown-unknowns. Using it requires a change to the baseline.
The approved, time-phased budget excluding management reserve; it includes contingency reserves.
terms.formula: Cost baseline = Σ work-package estimates + contingency reserves

terms.definition: Adjusting the timing of planned expenditure so it stays within the periodic funding ceilings (for example annual budget releases).
Money already spent that cannot be recovered. It should not influence decisions about the future — only future costs and benefits matter.
Considering the total cost of ownership — design, build, operate, maintain, dispose — rather than build cost alone. Cheap pavement can be expensive runway.
Determining the cause and degree of difference between baseline and actual performance, and deciding whether corrective action is needed.
An uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive (opportunity) or negative (threat) effect on one or more objectives.
A risk that would have a negative effect on objectives. Responses: avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept, escalate.
A risk that would have a positive effect on objectives. Responses: exploit, share, enhance, accept, escalate.
The repository of identified risks with their probability, impact, score, owner, trigger, response and status.
A hierarchical representation of risk sources (technical, external, organisational, project management) used to prompt identification.
A grid that combines probability and impact scores to prioritise risks into high, medium and low bands.
terms.formula: Risk score = probability score × impact score

terms.definition: Prioritising risks by assessing probability, impact and other characteristics on ordinal scales. Fast and subjective.
Numerically analysing the combined effect of risks on objectives using EMV, decision trees and Monte Carlo simulation.
The probability-weighted value of a risk. Threats carry negative EMV, opportunities positive. Summed EMV informs the contingency reserve.
A diagram of decisions, chance events and outcomes; rolling back EMVs from right to left identifies the option with the best expected value.
The chosen way to deal with a risk. Threats: avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept, escalate. Opportunities: exploit, share, enhance, accept, escalate.
Threat response that eliminates the threat or protects the project from it, typically by changing the plan (e.g. rerouting haul roads away from the residential edge).
Threat response that shifts ownership and impact to a third party — insurance, performance bonds, fixed-price contracts. The risk does not disappear.
Threat response that reduces the probability and/or impact to an acceptable threshold, such as night paving in summer heat.
Response that acknowledges a risk without proactive action. Active acceptance sets aside contingency; passive acceptance does nothing.
Response used when a risk is outside the project's authority or scope; it is passed to the programme, portfolio or sponsor who owns it.
Opportunity response that ensures the opportunity is realised, for instance assigning the best crew to capture an early-completion bonus.
Opportunity response that increases the probability or impact of an opportunity.
Opportunity response that allocates ownership to a third party best able to capture the benefit, such as a joint venture.
The risk that remains after a response has been implemented.
A new risk created directly by implementing a risk response — e.g. night paving reduces heat risk but raises safety and noise risk.
An early-warning sign that a risk is about to occur or has occurred, such as a dust-storm forecast or a supplier missing a delivery.
The named person responsible for monitoring a risk and implementing its response.
The degree of uncertainty an organisation is willing to accept in anticipation of a reward. Risk thresholds turn appetite into measurable limits.
A measure of acceptable variation around an objective (e.g. no more than 5% cost overrun) above which a risk must be actively treated.
The aggregate potential effect of the open risks, often expressed as the sum of their EMVs.
An unplanned response to a threat that has occurred and for which no response had been prepared.
A response planned in advance and executed only if a specified trigger occurs. A fallback plan is used if the contingency plan itself fails.
A record of current problems (risks that have happened, disputes, blockers) with an owner, due date and status.
The degree to which a set of inherent characteristics fulfils requirements. Grade is a category; low grade can be acceptable, low quality never is.
A category assigned to deliverables having the same functional use but different technical characteristics.
Process-focused activities that give confidence that quality requirements will be met — audits, process reviews, method statements.
Product-focused inspection and testing of deliverables to verify they meet requirements — cores, cubes, compaction tests, friction runs.
A structured, independent review to determine whether project activities comply with policies, processes and procedures.
Examining a work product to determine whether it conforms to documented standards. More inspection lowers external failure but raises appraisal cost.
All costs incurred over the product life cycle by investment in preventing non-conformance (prevention, appraisal) and by failing to conform (internal and external failure).
terms.formula: CoQ = prevention + appraisal + internal failure + external failure

terms.definition: A time-ordered chart of a process measure with a centre line and upper and lower control limits (usually ±3σ). Points outside the limits or non-random patterns show a process out of control.
Boundaries of common-cause variation calculated from the process data, typically ±3σ from the mean. They describe the voice of the process.
Boundaries set by the customer or standard (USL, LSL). They describe the voice of the customer and are not the same as control limits.
How well a stable process fits within the specification limits.

Decision rules for detecting non-random patterns on a control chart: (1) one point beyond 3σ; (2) two of three consecutive points beyond 2σ on the same side; (3) four of five beyond 1σ on the same side; (4) eight consecutive points on one side of the centre line.
A heuristic that seven or more consecutive points on one side of the mean (or trending in one direction) indicate a non-random cause even if within control limits.
Natural, random variation inherent in a stable process. Reacting to it as if it were special (tampering) makes things worse.
Variation from a specific, identifiable source outside the normal process — a bad batch, an uncalibrated gauge. It must be investigated.
A bar chart ordered by frequency with a cumulative line, used to focus on the vital few causes that produce most defects (the 80/20 principle).
The observation that roughly 80% of problems come from about 20% of causes.
A cause-and-effect (Ishikawa) diagram that organises potential causes of a problem into categories such as methods, materials, machines, people, measurement and environment.
An analytical technique to determine the basic underlying reason for a variance, defect or risk, so the fix prevents recurrence.
Asking "why?" repeatedly (about five times) to move from symptom to root cause.
A bar chart showing the distribution of numerical data, used to see the shape and spread of a quality measure.
A plot of two variables to reveal correlation, such as asphalt laying temperature against compaction density.
A formal record that a deliverable or process does not meet its specification, with disposition (rework, repair, accept as-is, reject) and corrective action.
Action taken to bring a defective component into conformance. Rework is an internal failure cost and often hits the critical path.
The Shewhart/Deming continuous-improvement cycle: plan a change, do it, check the results, act to standardise or adjust.
Ongoing incremental improvement of processes and products; in agile teams it is built into retrospectives.
Japanese term for continuous small improvements involving everyone in the organisation.
A data-driven quality approach aiming at very low defect rates by reducing process variation, often using the DMAIC cycle.
Choosing part of a population for inspection; attribute sampling counts pass/fail, variable sampling measures on a continuous scale.

A responsibility assignment matrix showing who is Responsible (does the work), Accountable (single owner who signs off), Consulted (two-way input) and Informed (kept up to date) for each deliverable. Exactly one A per row.
A grid that shows the project resources assigned to each work package; RACI is the most common form.
Team development model with five stages: forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning. Leaders adapt their style to the stage.
A document recording team values, agreements and operating guidelines — communication norms, decision making, conflict handling.
Expectations regarding acceptable behaviour by team members, usually captured in the team charter.
A leadership style that puts the team first: removing impediments, coaching, shielding the team from distraction and enabling self-organisation.
The ability to recognise and manage your own emotions and those of others — essential for negotiation and conflict resolution.
Techniques for resolving conflict: collaborate/problem-solve (win-win), compromise, smooth/accommodate, force/direct, withdraw/avoid. Collaboration addresses the root cause.
Discussion aimed at reaching agreement; principled negotiation separates people from the problem and focuses on interests, not positions.
Frameworks such as Maslow's hierarchy, Herzberg's hygiene and motivating factors, and McGregor's Theory X/Y, used to understand what drives team performance.
A group with a shared goal whose members work mostly from different locations, relying on digital communication.
Placing team members in the same physical location (a site office or war room) to improve communication.
A calendar identifying working days, shifts and availability of each resource, including holidays and seasonal restrictions.
An individual, group or organisation that may affect, be affected by, or perceive itself to be affected by the project.
A document listing stakeholders with their role, interest, influence, expectations and classification.
A 2×2 classification of stakeholders: manage closely (high power, high interest), keep satisfied (high power, low interest), keep informed (low power, high interest), monitor (low, low).
Stakeholder classification by power, legitimacy and urgency; stakeholders with all three are "definitive" and demand immediate attention.
A matrix comparing each stakeholder's current engagement level (unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive, leading) with the desired level, to plan actions that close the gap.
The plan describing strategies and actions to promote productive involvement of stakeholders in decisions and execution.
Describes what information goes to whom, when, how, in what format and by whom — and how it will be stored and escalated.
The number of potential communication paths in a team; it grows quadratically with team size, which is why communication planning matters.
Information sent to specific recipients (emails, letters, reports) — it does not guarantee it was read or understood.
Information placed where recipients can access it at their discretion — intranet, dashboards, notice boards.
Real-time, multidirectional exchange — meetings, calls, workshops. Best for complex or sensitive issues.
A periodic report of where the project stands: progress, EVM indices, forecast, top risks, issues, decisions needed. Good reports lead with the decision required.
A formal, accessible process for affected communities to raise concerns and receive a response — essential on infrastructure projects next to neighbourhoods.
The ongoing acceptance of a project by the local community and other stakeholders; it can be lost far faster than it is earned.
The process of reviewing all change requests, approving or rejecting them, and managing changes to deliverables, documents and the project management plan.
A formal proposal to modify a document, deliverable or baseline. It is analysed for impact on scope, time, cost, quality and risk before a decision.
A formally constituted group responsible for reviewing, evaluating, approving, deferring or rejecting changes and recording the decisions.
Controlling the specifications and versions of deliverables and documents so everyone builds to the current approved version.
A list of all change requests submitted and their current status.
An intentional activity that realigns the performance of the project work with the plan.
An intentional activity that ensures the future performance of the project work is aligned with the plan.
An intentional activity to modify a non-conforming product or component.
A record of key decisions, who made them, when and why — invaluable when the same question returns months later.
Processes to purchase or acquire products, services or results from outside the project team: plan, conduct and control procurements.
Deciding whether work should be done in-house or purchased, considering cost, capability, risk, capacity and strategic importance.
Families of contracts that allocate risk differently: fixed price (seller carries cost risk), cost-reimbursable (buyer carries it) and time and materials (hybrid).
Contract with a set price for a well-defined scope; the seller carries most cost risk. Best when scope is clear and stable.
Fixed-price contract with a target cost, target profit, share ratio and ceiling price; the seller earns more profit by beating the target.
terms.formula: Final price = actual cost + target fee + share × (target cost − actual cost), capped at ceiling

terms.definition: In an FPIF contract, the cost above which the seller bears all further cost overrun.
terms.formula: PTA = (ceiling price − target price) / buyer share + target cost

terms.term: Fixed Price with Economic Price Adjustment
terms.definition: Fixed price with an adjustment clause tied to an index (e.g. bitumen or steel prices) for long contracts exposed to inflation.
Cost-reimbursable contract where the seller is paid allowable costs plus a fixed fee; the buyer carries the cost risk. Suited to uncertain scope.
Cost-reimbursable contract with an incentive fee based on meeting cost targets, with savings or overruns shared by an agreed ratio.
Cost-reimbursable contract where the fee is awarded subjectively by the buyer based on performance criteria.
Hybrid contract paying unit rates for labour and materials; quick to start, but needs a not-to-exceed limit to control cost.
A procurement document asking sellers for proposals on how they would deliver a solution; used when technical approach matters as much as price. RFQ is for price only; RFI gathers information.
A meeting with all prospective sellers before bids are submitted, so everyone receives the same information.
Weighted criteria (technical approach, experience, schedule, price, financial capacity) used to score proposals objectively.
A decision technique that rates options against weighted criteria and sums the results to rank them.
A narrative description of the products, services or results to be delivered under a contract.

A request, demand or assertion of rights by a seller against a buyer (or vice versa) under the contract, often over changed conditions or delay. Alternative dispute resolution is preferred to litigation.
Resolving contract disputes through negotiation, mediation or arbitration rather than the courts.
A percentage of each payment withheld from the contractor until completion or the end of the defects-liability period, as security for performance.
A guarantee by a bank or surety that compensates the buyer if the contractor fails to perform.
Completing each procurement: verifying deliverables, settling claims, releasing retention, archiving records and capturing lessons.
A mindset and family of approaches defined by the Agile Manifesto's values and principles: individuals and interactions, working results, customer collaboration and responding to change.

A lightweight agile framework with three accountabilities (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers), five events (Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Retrospective) and three artifacts (Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment).
A fixed-length timebox (here 14 days) in which a usable increment is created. Scope may be clarified but the sprint goal does not change.
The event that starts a sprint: the team selects backlog items, crafts a sprint goal and plans how to deliver it.
A short daily meeting (Daily Scrum) for the team to inspect progress toward the sprint goal and adapt the plan; classic prompts are done yesterday, plan today, blockers.
Event at the end of a sprint where the team demonstrates the increment to stakeholders and the backlog is adapted.
Event where the team inspects how the last sprint went — people, process, tools — and commits to improvements.
The person accountable for maximising the value of the product by ordering the product backlog.
The person accountable for the team's effectiveness: coaching Scrum, facilitating events and removing impediments. A servant leader.
An ordered list of everything that might be needed in the product; the single source of work for the team.
The sprint goal, the backlog items selected for the sprint and the plan for delivering them.
Ongoing activity of adding detail, estimates and order to backlog items. Also called grooming.
A short description of a feature from the user's perspective: "As a <role> I want <capability> so that <benefit>", with acceptance criteria.
Checklist for good user stories: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.
A relative unit of effort and complexity used to size user stories, often on a Fibonacci-like scale.
A consensus estimation technique in which team members reveal story-point cards simultaneously and discuss outliers.
The amount of work (story points) a team completes per sprint. Use the average of recent sprints to forecast; never compare velocity between teams.
terms.formula: Sprints remaining ≈ remaining points / average velocity

terms.definition: A chart of remaining work against time with an ideal line; above the line means behind.
A chart of completed work against time with a separate scope line, which makes scope changes visible.
A shared checklist of criteria an increment must meet to be considered complete — the team-wide quality bar.
Criteria a backlog item must meet before the team will take it into a sprint.
A concrete, usable step toward the product goal that meets the Definition of Done.
The smallest version of a product that delivers value and validates assumptions with real users.
A flow-based method that visualises work on a board, limits work in progress and manages flow, pulling new work only when capacity frees up.
A cap on the number of items allowed in a workflow state. Limiting work in progress reduces multitasking, exposes bottlenecks and shortens cycle time.
terms.formula: Little's Law: cycle time = WIP / throughput

terms.definition: A queueing relationship: average cycle time equals average work in progress divided by average throughput.
The elapsed time from when work starts on an item until it is finished. Lead time runs from request to delivery.
The elapsed time from a request entering the system to its delivery — what the customer experiences. In procurement, the time from order to delivery.
The number of work items completed per unit of time.
A stacked-area chart of items in each workflow state over time; widening bands reveal bottlenecks.
Anything that blocks or slows the team. Removing impediments is the Scrum Master's job.
A fixed, maximum period for an activity; when the time is up, the activity ends.
A cross-functional team that decides internally who does what, when and how, within the constraints set by the organisation.
The future cost of rework caused by choosing an easy solution now instead of a better approach that would take longer.
A timeboxed research or prototyping story used to reduce uncertainty before estimating real work.
Knowledge gained during the project about what worked and what did not, captured throughout (not only at the end) and stored in the organisational process assets.
Formal sign-off by the customer or sponsor that the deliverables meet the acceptance criteria, which triggers handover.
Transfer of completed deliverables, documentation, warranties and responsibility from the project to operations.
A review some months after handover to check whether the expected benefits are being realised.
A period after completion during which the contractor must remedy defects at their own cost; retention is usually released at its end.
In scheduling software such as MS Project, auto-scheduled tasks are calculated from dependencies and calendars; manually scheduled tasks keep the dates typed in.
In MS Project, a parent task that rolls up the dates, work and cost of its subtasks; it mirrors a WBS element.
In MS Project, which of duration, work or units stays fixed when one of the others changes (Work = Duration × Units).
An MS Project option in which adding resources to a task shortens its duration while total work stays constant.
In MS Project, a date restriction on a task such as As Soon As Possible, Start No Earlier Than or Must Finish On. Hard constraints override logic and can create negative float.
In MS Project, a target date that flags a task when it is late but, unlike a hard constraint, does not move the task.
An MS Project view that shows baseline bars beneath current bars so slippage is visible at a glance.
The Microsoft Project XML data interchange format; this simulator exports the live schedule as MSPDI so it can be opened in MS Project.
An MS Project view listing resources with type (work, material, cost), maximum units and rates.

A structured programme that prepares people, processes and systems to operate a new or expanded airport facility, including familiarisation, trials with volunteers and a controlled transfer from the project to operations.
An ICAO two-element code that links airfield design to the aircraft it serves: a number (1–4) for reference field length and a letter (A–F) for wingspan.
Aerodrome reference code letter for aircraft with a wingspan of 24 m up to but not including 36 m — typical single-aisle airliners.
Aerodrome reference code letter for aircraft with a wingspan of 52 m up to but not including 65 m — large twin-aisle airliners. It drives runway and taxiway widths, separations and stand sizes.
A row of four light units beside the runway that show pilots whether they are on the approach slope: two red and two white means on slope; more white is high, more red is low.
A precision radio navigation aid giving lateral guidance (localiser) and vertical guidance (glide path) to a runway, allowing approaches in low visibility.
The ILS component, an antenna array beyond the runway end, that gives lateral guidance along the extended centreline. It must be protected from obstacles and vehicles.
A cleared, graded area beyond the runway strip at each end that reduces damage if an aircraft undershoots or overruns. ICAO sets a minimum length and recommends a longer one.
A defined area including the runway (and stopway) that is graded and kept free of obstacles to reduce risk to aircraft running off the runway.
The airport emergency service equipped to respond to aircraft accidents. The required category depends on aircraft size, and response-time objectives apply to any point on the runway.
Imaginary surfaces around a runway that define the airspace to be kept free of obstacles — cranes on an airside construction site need specific clearance.
Notice to Air Missions: an official notice of temporary changes such as runway closures, displaced thresholds or works in progress.
A runway threshold located at a point other than the runway end, often used temporarily during works so aircraft can continue to operate on a shortened runway.
An airside construction plan that defines phasing, work areas, haul routes, closures and safety measures so construction and flight operations can coexist.
Any object on the movement area that could damage aircraft — loose aggregate, bolts, plastic. Construction sites must run FOD sweeps and inspections.
The ICAO number expressing the bearing strength of a pavement for unrestricted operations, compared with the aircraft classification rating (ACR). It replaced ACN/PCN.
A configuration of lights extending from the threshold into the approach area that helps pilots transition from instruments to visual references.
The area of an airport where aircraft park for boarding, loading, refuelling and maintenance; its stands are sized by aerodrome reference code.
Vehicles and equipment that service aircraft between flights — tugs, belt loaders, fuel bowsers, ground power units.
A systematic approach to managing aviation safety: policy, risk management, assurance and promotion. Airside works are assessed under it.
The part of an airport beyond security screening and access control, including the movement area. Work here needs permits, escorts and coordination with air traffic control.
The public part of an airport before security — forecourt, car parks, access roads and the public areas of the terminal.
A study that predicts the environmental and social effects of a project — noise, air quality, land, water, communities — and sets mitigation before approval.
Using analytics and AI agents to monitor data, forecast, draft communications and recommend actions, while a human remains accountable for decisions.
A design in which an AI may recommend or prepare an action but a person must review and approve it before it takes effect. Every MEHRAN action works this way.
The ability to show why an AI produced a given recommendation — the rule, data and threshold behind it — so people can trust, challenge or reject it.
When a generative AI states something fluent but unsupported or false. Grounding answers in live data and saying "not in the data" are the main defences.
Protecting personal and confidential information. In this simulator an API key stays in session storage only and no project data leaves the browser unless you enable live mode.
